title: Dynamic monitoring of circulating tumor DNA to analyze genetic characteristics and resistance profile of lorlatinib in ALK positive previously treated NSCLC
author: Xiya Ma; Kun Zhang; Jing Xu; Hongjun Gao; Shaoxing Yang; Haifeng Qin; Hong Wang; Fang Gao; Xiaoqing Liu
text:
Abstract
Background
To dynamically monitor the changes of genomic characteristics during lorlatinib treatment and analyze the resistance profile of lorlatinib in ALK‐positive advanced Chinese patients with non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with first‐ and second‐generation ALK inhibitor resistance.
Methods
Ten eligible patients who were from a phase 2 study in China and admitted to the Fifth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital were analyzed. Blood samples were collected for next‐generation sequencing (NGS) to characterize genetic variation at baseline, during treatment, and after disease progression.
Results
Among the 10 patients treated with lorlatinib, objective response rate (ORR) was 50%. The median progression‐free survival (PFS) was 13.3 months, and median overall survival (OS) was 15.6 months. At baseline, the mutation frequency of ALK in circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) was higher in the group who received two lines of previous anaplastic lymphoma kinase‐tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ALK‐TKIs), and a similar trend was observed for TP53. After one follow‐up cycle, the decreased variant allele frequency (VAF) had a trend to be predictive for responses. In six patients in which blood samples had been taken after lorlatinib resistance, ALK compound mutations were found in three patients (50%), which were G1202R/L1196M, L1196M/D1203N, and G1202R/F1174C. The DNMT3A N403Tfs*4, ERCC3 E259D, and GNAS p.A436_P459del variants were only detected after progression in two of the other three patients without ALK compound mutations.
Conclusions
The dynamic changes of genomic characteristics during lorlatinib treatment revealed the mutation landscape of Chinese patients with NSCLC after ALK‐TKI resistance, indicated that the resistance profile of lorlatinib were heterogeneous, which laid the foundation for subsequent treatment to overcome lorlatinib resistance.
Keywords: ALK, ctDNA, genetic characteristics, lorlatinib, resistance
Blood samples from 10 patients treated with lorlatinib were collected for next‐generation sequencing to characterize genetic variation at baseline, during treatment, and after disease progression. After one follow‐up cycle, the decreased variant allele frequency had a trend to be predictive for responses. In six patients in which blood samples had been taken after lorlatinib resistance, ALK compound mutations were found in three patients (50%), which were G1202R/L1196M, L1196M/D1203N, and G1202R/F1174C.
INTRODUCTION
Lung cancer is the cancer with the highest incidence and high mortality in China. 1 Non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with ALK gene rearrangement account for about 3%–5%, and are sensitive to treatment with anaplastic lymphoma kinase‐tyrosine kinase inhibitors (ALK‐TKIs). 2 , 3 Crizotinib is the earliest first‐generation ALK inhibitor approved for advanced NSCLC among ALK‐TKIs, which has been previously reported to have a higher tumor response rate and progression‐free survival than standard chemotherapy. 4 , 5 Ceritinib, brigatinib, alectinib, and ensartinib are second‐generation ALK‐TKIs, 6 , 7 all of which have been approved and marketed in China. The third‐generation ALK‐TKI lorlatinib was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2019 for the posterior line treatment of NSCLC after first‐ or second‐generation ALK inhibitor resistance, and was approved in March 2021 for first‐line ALK‐positive advanced NSCLC patients. 8
Phase II studies of lorlatinib, a third‐generation ALK inhibitor, have shown strong and long‐lasting antitumor effects in previously treated patients with ALK‐positive NSCLC. 8 , 9 Although ALK‐TKIs are highly effective, patients may develop tumor progression due to acquired resistance. The mechanisms of resistance to first‐ and second‐generation ALK‐TKIs have been widely studied, 10 , 11 while studies on the resistance mechanism to third‐generation ALK‐TKIs remains limited. The multicenter clinical study reported by Yoda et al. showed that the probability of ALK compound mutation after lorlatinib resistance was 35% (7/20). 12 Recondo et al. identified three novel ALK compound mutations (F1174L/G1202R, L1196M/D1203N, and C1156Y/G1269A), as well as a novel bypass mechanism: loss of NF2 function. 13 The above studies showed that the resistance mechanisms to lorlatinib are diverse and complex. Therefore, more studies are needed to further explore the mechanism of resistance to lorlatinib.
Dynamic monitoring of plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is a promising noninvasive strategy that can repeatedly evaluate genomic profiles, discover and identify drug resistance mechanisms, and predict efficacy. 14 , 15 , 16 Combined with our clinical work, we observed the efficacy and safety of lorlatinib treatment in ALK‐positive advanced NSCLC patients resistant to the first‐ and second‐generation ALK inhibitor, and analyzed the dynamic changes of gene characteristics before and after lorlatinib treatment by targeted ctDNA sequencing. Our study aimed to lay a foundation for guiding the further treatment after drug resistance to multiple ALK‐TKIs.
METHODS
Patients
A total of 10 eligible patients who were from a phase 2 study in China (NCT03909971) and admitted to the Department of Pulmonary Oncology, the Fifth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital from June to December 2019 were analyzed. The main inclusion criteria were: (1) Diagnosis of locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC. (2) Positivity for ALK gene rearrangement (immunochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization assay, reverse transcriptase‐polymerase chain reaction or next‐generation sequencing [NGS] were selected as the detection method). (3) Had received lorlatinib for at least 42 days after progression on previous crizotinib and/or second‐generation ALK inhibitors. (4) There must be at least one measurable extracranial target lesion determined according to RECIST version 1.1 that had not previously received radiotherapy. All patients received lorlatinib treatment every 3 weeks as a treatment cycle. The initial dose was 100 mg once a day, and the dose was adjusted appropriately according to toxicity. This study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the Fifth Medical Center of PLA General Hospital. All tests were carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Evaluation of efficacy and safety
Imaging assessment of the tumor site was performed by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging in all enrolled patients at each follow‐up cycle which included two treatment cycles (T1, 6 weeks) until disease progression. All target lesions were evaluated according to the Response Evaluation Criteria for Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. The objective response rate (ORR) was the percentage of cases with complete response (CR) and partial response (PR) to the evaluable cases. Progression‐free survival (PFS) was defined as the time between initiation of lorlatinib therapy and the onset of disease progression or death from any cause. Duration of response (DOR) was defined as the time from the first efficacy assessment of CR or PR to the first assessment of progressive disease (PD) or death from any cause. Overall survival (OS) was defined as the time from the start of lorlatinib therapy to death.
The grading of side effects associated with lorlatinib treatment was performed according to the Generic Terminology Standard for Adverse Events, version 5.0 (CTCAE 5.0). The date of last follow‐up was January 31, 2022.
Sample preparation and 556 gene targeted sequencing
For sample preparation, 10 mL of peripheral blood samples were collected at baseline before treatment with lorlatinib, during treatment, and at the time of disease progression. A total of 38 peripheral blood samples were initially centrifuged at low temperature and then separated and frozen.
For targeted sequencing, the ctDNA and germline DNA from the same patient were detected by next‐generation sequencing (Tongshu Biotech). The ctDNA was extracted from plasma according to the manufacturer's instructions (HiPure circulating DNA midi kit, Magen). Germline DNA was extracted from blood lymphocytes using HiPure blood DNA mini kit (Magen). A NadPrep DNA library preparation kit (Nanodigmbio) was used to prepare libraries for the Illumina sequencing platform. A NadPrep Hybrid Capture Reagents kit (Nanodigmbio) was used for hybridization capture–based target enrichment. The captured libraries sequencing was performed as paired‐end reads on the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform.
Data processing
The sequence data were filtered by Fastp (version 0.20.0) and aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using Burrows–Wheeler Aligner (BWA, version: 0.7.12‐r1039). Single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and insertion/deletion (Indel) were detected using vardict‐java (version 1.7.0‐0) and Mutect2 of GATK4 (version 4.1.8.1). Structural variations were detected using factera (version 1.4.4). After filtering, those variants were then annotated by Ensembl's variant effect predictor (VEP, version 104).
Definition of possibly damaging mutations
The mutations of driver genes were defined to be possibly damaging as follows: (i) Nonsense, frame‐shift, and splice‐site mutations; and (ii) missense mutations either with FATHMM‐MKL score >0.5 in the annotation of Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC), or identified to be functionally damaging by two or more functional analysis algorithms: predication score 0.0–0.05 by SIFT, “possibly damaging” or “probably damaging” by Polyphen2, “medium” or “high” by Mutation Assessor, or predication score >0.5 by FATHMM‐MKL.
Statistical analysis
Fisher's exact test was used to compare the frequency data between two groups. Kaplan–Meier survival analysis was performed, and the resulting curves were compared using the log‐rank test. For all statistical tests, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
RESULTS
Characteristics of patients
A total of 11 ALK‐positive advanced NSCLC patients who were treated with lorlatinib after progression on previous first‐ and/or second‐generation ALK inhibitors in our department from June to December 2019 were enrolled in this study. Among them, one patient was excluded from the analysis because of rapid progression of disease and respiratory failure in the short term after lorlatinib administration, and his family declined continuation of further treatment. A total of 10 patients were eligible, and 38 peripheral blood samples were collected from all eligible patients.
The median age of the 10 patients was 50 years (27–69 years), of which only one had adenosquamous carcinoma and the rest were adenocarcinoma. Five patients received crizotinib only, and the other five patients had received two‐line ALK‐TKIs. The clinical characteristics and gene variants of the patients are shown in Table 1.

Therapeutic efficacy and safety of lorlatinib
Among 10 patients treated with lorlatinib, the best response was PR in five cases (50%), stable disease (SD) in five cases (50%), and the ORR was 50%. At last follow‐up, seven patients had disease progression. The median PFS was 13.3 months (95% CI: 10.8–15.8), and the median DOR was 12.8 months (95% CI: 11.1–14.5). To date, the disease has not progressed in three patients (30%), and the duration of treatment has exceeded 32 months. At last follow‐up, a total of six patients had died, and the median OS was 15.6 months (95% CI: 0–39.6) with posterior line lorlatinib. The remaining four patients who were still alive were from the crizotinib‐only group.
The adverse events (AEs) reported for all grades are summarized in Table 2, including hypertriglyceridemia (100%), hypercholesterolemia (100%), increased weight (70%), elevated ALT (50%), anemia (50%), hyperglycemia (40%), elevated AST (40%), etc. Grade 3–4 treatment‐related adverse events were reported in 90% of patients, including hypertriglyceridemia (50%), hypercholesterolemia (40%), increased weight (40%), hyperglycemia (10%), and anemia (10%). A total of four serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported by January 31, 2022 (Table 3). One case had an old fracture of the right ulna olecranon without discontinuation of lorlatinib. One case had fever and respiratory failure and died at home. The cause of death was unclear, and it was considered to be associated with disease progression. One case had a pulmonary embolism which was considered to be associated with progressive disease. One case died of unknown causes, and there was insufficient evidence to link it to lorlatinib.

Gene variation analysis with ctDNA before treatment with lorlatinib
The targeted sequencing results showed that 68 variants in 43 genes were identified from ctDNA in peripheral blood samples from 10 patients treated with lorlatinib at baseline, of which 28 were driver genes. Most of the variant classification were missense mutation in those patients treated previously with lorlatinib (Figure 1a). C > T, T > C, and T > G variants were predominant (Figure 1b). The mutated somatic driver genes detected in at least two baseline samples were KMT2C (6/10, 60%), TP53 (5/10, 50%), ALK (4/10, 40%), NOTCH2 (3/10, 30%), FOXL2 (3/10, 30%), and EPAS1 (2/10, 20%) and GNAS (2/10, 20%), KRAS (2/10, 20%) and TGFBR2 (2/10, 20%) (Figure 1c).
After the failure of first‐ and second‐generation ALK inhibitor treatment, a total of four patients (4/10) had ALK secondary mutations detected in ctDNA, and all received two lines of previous ALK‐TKI treatment, G1202R in patient P5, D1203N/L1196M/R1192P/F1174C/F1174V/C1156Y/G1128A in patient P6, G1202R/F1174C in P7, L1196M in patient P8. The mutation frequency of ALK and TP53 in the group who received two‐line previous ALK‐TKI treatment was higher than that in the group who received only crizotinib treatment (ALK 80% vs. 0%; TP53 80% vs. 20%), but the difference for TP53 was not statistically significant due to the limited number of patients (Figure 1d).
The distribution of variant genes at baseline was different in the groups with different best response. In the group with the best PR response, the recurrent mutated genes at baseline were KMT2C (4/5, 80%), NOTCH2 (3/5, 60%), TP53 (3/5, 60%), FOXL2 (2/5, 40%), ALK (2/5, 40%), EPAS1 (2/5, 40%), and KRAS (2/5, 40%). In the group with the best SD response, the recurrent mutated genes were KMT2C (40%), ALK (40%), and TP53 (40%) (Figure 1c). There was a trend for the variant frequencies of NOTCH2, KRAS, and KMT2C to be higher in the PR group (60% vs. 0%, 40% vs. 0%, 80% vs. 40%), although these differences were not significant due to the limited number of patients.
The association between recurrently mutated genes, previous ALK‐TKI treatment, and PFS was also investigated. TP53 mutations and ALK mutations were associated with poor PFS in these patients (Figure S1a,b). Compared with patients who received only crizotinib treatment, the patients who received crizotinib and ceritinib were shown to have a poor PFS by analysis of these 10 patients. Compared with patients who received only crizotinib treatment, the patients who received two lines of previous ALK‐TKIs were also associated with poor PFS, including four patients who received crizotinib and ceritinib treatment and one patient who received crizotinib and alectinib treatment (Figure S1c,d).
Dynamic changes of ctDNA during the treatment of lorlatinib
In addition to baseline, a series of ctDNA tests were also carried out during lorlatinib treatment (Figure 2), and the results showed that ctDNA VAF at T1 (C3D1) was reduced from baseline in six patients, including four patients with PR and two patients with SD. The VAF of ctDNA in the remaining four patients at T1 was not decreased from baseline, including one case of PR and three cases of SD. Among the overall patients, the three patients with the largest decrease in mean VAF had the best efficacy evaluation of PR (Figure 3).
Detection of variations in ctDNA from lorlatinib resistant patients
At the last follow‐up, seven patients had disease progression. We investigated the resistance variants in ctDNA from six patients with progression who had blood collected after progression on lorlatinib (Figure 4).
The results showed that ALK compound mutations were detected in three patients (50%). Patient P5 developed the ALK compound mutation G1202R/L1196M after treatment with lorlatinib, which was not detected in T0, T1, and T2 blood (Figure 4b). Patient P6 harbored the ALK compound mutation L1196M/D1203N after lorlatinib progression which showed a sharply elevated mutant frequency than that in T0 blood (Figure 4c). KRAS G13C, KRAS G12S, KMT2D H760‐P777del, and EPAS1 S474T mutations first occurred after lorlatinib progression in patient P6. Although only ALK G1202R was found after lorlatinib progression in patient 7, the compound mutation G1202R/F1174C was found in T0 blood (Figure 4d). The NOTCH2 P227H, POLD1 D27del, and ATRX E1445_E1464del variants first occurred after progression on lorlatinib in patient P7.
No ALK compound mutation was found in the other three resistant patients. In patient P2, DNMT3A N403Tfs*4 was only detected at T2 when the tumor progressed (Figure 4a). In patient P9, ERCC3 E259D and GNAS p.A436_P459del were present after progression on lorlatinib (Figure 4e). The VAF level of the TP53 E271K mutation increased to 6.3% after lorlatinib progression in patient P10 which was only 0.7% in T0 blood (Figure 4f). The ALK mutations related to lorlatinib resistance and other first occurred possibly damaging mutations after lorlatinib resistance are shown in Table 1.
DISCUSSION
We not only observed the efficacy and safety of lorlatinib in 10 patients resistant to first‐and second‐generation ALK‐TKI treatment, but also dynamically monitored the genetic characteristics of these patients before and after lorlatinib treatment by ctDNA sequencing.
The newly published results of the phase II study on lorlatinib in a Chinese population showed that the ORR of patients resistant to first‐and second‐generation ALK inhibitor was 47.6% (20/42), and the median PFS was 5.6 months. 9 The phase I clinical study on lorlatinib showed that among ALK‐positive patients, the ORR was 46% (19/41); among those who had received ≥2 TKIs, the ORR was 42% (11/26). 17 Similar to previous studies, our results showed that the ORR was 50% in 10 patients treated with lorlatinib, and the treatment duration was more than 32 months due to the stable disease in three patients. The average age of the three patients previously only treated with crizotinib was 36 years old, and ALK mutations were not detected in ctDNA before lorlatinib treatment. In addition, one‐line previous ALK‐TKI treatment and negative ALK mutations were shown to be associated with better PFS by the analysis of the 10 patients in our study. Thus, one‐line previous ALK‐TKI treatment, younger age, and negative ALK mutations in ctDNA at baseline, may be predicative indicators for long‐term benefits from lorlatinib treatment.
Similar to previous studies, 9 , 18 the most common AEs observed after lorlatinib treatment were hypertriglyceridemia and hypercholesterolemia. Although the dysregulation of lipid metabolism is common, it is not a cause for great concern because it can be restored by drug management. The study reported no permanent discontinuation or treatment‐related deaths due to treatment‐related AEs. All SAEs were not confirmed to be associated with lorlatinib treatment. This indicates that lorlatinib has an acceptable safety in Chinese ALK‐positive NSCLC.
At baseline, we analyzed the tumor‐related mutations of lorlatinib treatment by ctDNA targeted sequencing. In other words, the mutations after progression on previous first‐and second‐generation ALK‐TKIs were investigated. In baseline ctDNA, ALK mutations were observed in three patients who had received previous crizotinib and ceritinib treatment; that is, p.G1202R in patient P5, p.D1203N, p.L1196M, p.R1192P, p.F1174C, p.F1174V, p.C1156Y, and p.G1128A in patient P6, p.G1202R and p.F1174C in patient P7. The ALK p.L1196M mutation was detected in patient P8 who had previously received crizotinib and alectinib treatment. The resistance of ALK p.G1202R, p.F1174C and p.G1128A mutations to ceritinib has been supported by several studies in recent years. 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 The ALK p.L1196M mutation was found to be resistant to crizotinib and remained moderately sensitive to alectinib. 23 Based on this, it is hypothesized that the disease progression in patient P8 before lorlatinib treatment was related to ALK mutation. Notably, after patient P2 was detected positive for the ALK gene rearrangement 11 years ago, the long‐term benefits of successive first‐and second‐generation ALK inhibitors were observed, including 24 months PFS for crizotinib and 62 months PFS for ceritinib. In addition, we analyzed the rapid progression of patient P2, which may be related to liver metastasis and TP53 mutation before lorlatinib treatment. TP53 mutations have been reported to be significantly associated with poor crizotinib PFS. 24 , 25 Similar to previous studies, patients with TP53 mutations were also associated with poor PFS by the analysis of 10 patients who received lorlatinib treatment in our study. However, the relationship of TP53 mutations and prognosis in patients who received lorlatinib treatment needs to be validated in further studies due to the limited number of patients in our study.
The mechanisms of lorlatinib resistance are diverse and complex, and ALK compound mutation is one of the mechanisms of lorlatinib resistance. 26 In this study, among the six patients whose blood was collected after lorlatinib progression, ALK compound mutations were found in three patients (50%) resistant to lorlatinib. It was a little higher than previous reports in which it was less than one‐third. 22 The compound ALK mutation L1196M/D1203N has been reported to induce a more than 300‐fold higher IC50, G1202R/F1196M induced a more than 500‐fold higher IC50, and they had high lorlatinib resistant features. 13 , 26 The G1202R/F1174C compound mutation was shown to induce a nearly 150‐fold higher IC50 in previous studies. 26 The G1202R/L1196M mutation in patient P5 first occurred after treatment with lorlatinib. The L1196M/D1203N mutation of patient P6 was significantly increased after lorlatinib progression. In patient P7, one component of the compound mutant G1202R/F1174C recurred after progression on lorlatinib. Although the ALK F1174C mutation was not detected in ctDNA, it may be related to the very low frequency of mutation in T0 blood, which was only 0.3%. In patient P7, the clinical outcomes achieved PR in the presence of compound mutations, and may be associated with the low mutation frequency of F1174C and the relatively weak resistance to this compound mutation compared with G1202R/L1196M and L1196M/D1203N mutations. Our findings support a critical role for ALK compound mutations in lorlatinib resistance. In addition to the L1196M/D1203N compound mutation, five other ALK mutations in baseline and one new occurred ALK mutation after progression on lorlatinib were detected in patient P6. Hu et al. found that multiple mutations mediated lorlatinib resistance. 27 Therefore, the poor PFS of patient P6 may be related to the strong resistance of multiple mutations to lorlatinib. However, these were all advanced NSCLC patients who received long‐term previous treatment with first‐ and/or second‐generation ALK inhibitors after the detection of ALK rearrangement. Tissue biopsy is an invasive and voluntary procedure for patients, and it is very difficult to obtain tumor tissue samples to further validate related ALK resistance mutations in practice. In future studies, we will strive to collect clinical data from eligible patients and obtain paired blood and tissue samples as much as possible, in order to further validate related ALK resistance mutations.
In the three patients who did not develop ALK compound variants after lorlatinib resistance, potentially damaging variants DNMT3A N403Tfs*4, ERCC3 E259D, and GNAS p.A436_P459del were only detected after progression in lorlatinib resistant patients P2 and P9. DNMT3A encodes a DNA methyltransferase, which is thought to play an important role in tumorigenesis and is associated with cancer progression. 28 ERCC3 is an important member of nucleotide excision repair overexpressed in a variety of cancers. 29 , 30 Mutations in genes involved in DNA repair have been linked to crizotinib resistance. GNAS is a cancer proto‐oncogene that exists in pituitary adenoma, appendiceal mucinous tumor and colon adenocarcinoma. 31 , 32 , 33 Therefore, three potentially damaging driver gene variants, DNMT3A N403Tfs*4, ERCC3 E259D, and GNAS p.A436_P459del, may be associated with resistance to lorlatinib.
In conclusion, in this study, we dynamically monitored the changes of genomic characteristics of NSCLC during lorlatinib treatment. Our study revealed the mutation landscape of NSCLC after ALK‐TKI resistance, indicated that ALK compound mutations were found in 50% of lorlatinib‐resistant Chinese patients and the resistance profile of lorlatinib were heterogeneous, which laid a foundation for further treatment of these patients.
